summary: An experimental specification of an RTP payload type for bundled MPEG-2 video and audio, so both can be sent together in one stream over RTP version 2.

eli5.summary: A way to wrap video and sound together in one package so they travel the internet side by side.

why bundle mpeg audio and video
how does bundled mpeg reduce overhead
what happens if you lose a packet with bundled mpeg
when should you use bundled mpeg vs separate streams
subtitle: Packaging MPEG-2 video and audio together in one RTP stream.

tldr.problem: When streaming MPEG-2 video and audio, sending them as separate RTP streams wastes bandwidth, uses two ports, and makes synchronization awkward.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2343 defines an RTP payload type that bundles MPEG-2 video and audio into a single stream, with a header indicating audio length and timing offset, so they travel together through the network.
tldr.outcome: Bundling saves bandwidth and simplifies receiver implementation for video-on-demand and similar applications, but sacrifices the modularity of separate streams.

today: RFC 2343 is an Experimental protocol and is not an Internet Standard. It defines a specialized RTP payload type suitable for video-on-demand and similar applications where bundling audio and video is advantageous.

sections.title: Why Bundle Audio and Video
sections.content:
MPEG-2 is an international standard for compressing video and audio. When sending MPEG-2 streams over the internet, RFC 2250 describes how to packetize the audio and video as separate RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) streams. However, for applications like video-on-demand (VOD), where audio and video are always used together, bundling them into a single RTP stream has significant advantages.

First, it uses a single port per program instead of two, increasing the number of streams a server can serve and improving client performance. Second, it provides implicit synchronization: since both streams are in the same packet, they are guaranteed to stay together. Third, it reduces overhead: larger video packets lower header percentage, and smaller audio-only packets can be avoided, saving about 1% bandwidth overall—which at 4 Mbps is 40 Kbps of improvement. Fourth, it can reduce receiver buffer requirements: when streams travel separately, they may experience different delays and buffers must be sized for the worst case. Fifth, it helps with bandwidth control for the overall program.
sections.eli5: Bundling the audio and video saves space, keeps them from getting out of sync, and makes the receiver simpler.

sections.title: Bundled Packet Structure
sections.content:
In the bundled format, each RTP packet contains video data followed by audio data. The video data must contain one or more complete slices (vertical sections of a video frame), and must begin with any MPEG sequence header, GOP (Group of Pictures) header or picture header that is present. The audio data is one or more complete audio frames that cover the time duration of the video segment in the packet.

For example, if a packet contains three 1/900-second slices of video, and the audio codec is Layer I MPEG audio at 44.1 kHz, one audio frame of 384/44100 seconds is sufficient. However, if the audio frame is longer than the video segment duration, subsequent packets may not include any audio frames until the accumulated video duration extends beyond the audio frame length. Alternatively, the application can repeat the latest audio frame in packets with no new audio data, for packet loss resilience.

The application (not the protocol) must ensure packets do not exceed the path MTU (maximum transmission unit) to avoid fragmentation. This approach simplifies the receiver but increases complexity on the transmitter side, since the transmitter must carefully choose slice sizes and packet boundaries.
sections.eli5: Pack video slices and audio frames together so they fit nicely in a network packet.

sections.title: BMPEG Header Fields
sections.content:
Each bundled MPEG (BMPEG) packet carries a 4-byte header after the standard RTP header. The header contains several fields. The P field (2 bits) indicates picture type: I-frame (intra, 0), P-frame (predictive, 1), or B-frame (bi-predictive, 2). The N bit (1 bit) signals whether any MPEG header data (sequence, GOP or picture header) differs from the previously sent headers; it is reset when headers are repeated. The MBZ (Must Be Zero) field is reserved.

The Audio Length field (10 bits) specifies the number of bytes of audio data in this packet. The receiver finds the audio by subtracting audio length from the total packet size. The Audio Offset field (16 bits, signed) gives the offset in audio samples between the start of the audio frame and the RTP timestamp for this packet. This allows approximately ±750 milliseconds offset at 44.1 kHz. For very low video frame rates (e.g., one frame per second), this offset may be insufficient and the payload type may not be suitable.

When B-frames are present, audio frames are not reordered with the video; they are packetized in transmission order. The audio offset remains relative to the timestamp in the packet containing that audio segment.
sections.eli5: A small header tells the receiver how much audio is in the packet and how the audio lines up with the video.

sections.title: Handling Packet Loss
sections.content:
Packet loss is detected from the RTP sequence number and timestamp. The extent of loss can be determined from the timestamp and the slice position (which can be read from fixed bit positions in the MPEG slice header). If lost data is only from slices within a single picture, the video decoder can be fed the new data after the loss and will normally repeat pixels from a previous picture. The audio frames must be played at the time indicated by the timestamp and audio offset of the received packet.

If new data after a loss is from a different picture (no complete picture is lost) and the N bit is zero, previously received headers for that picture type can be used with the new data. If N is set, it is advisable to skip data until a new picture start code is found, unless headers are available through another channel. If more than one picture is lost and headers are not available through other means, resynchronization to a new video sequence header is advisable.

The RFC also notes that if GOP headers are lost, B-pictures immediately following the loss may be incorrectly decoded for some edited video material, since there is no explicit picture counter in the payload format to detect such losses. To enable faster resynchronization after severe packet loss, frequent video sequence headers can be used.
sections.eli5: When packets are lost, the receiver can skip over the bad part and keep going with the next complete picture it finds.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the same security considerations as the RTP specification. Confidentiality of the media streams is achieved through encryption. Since MPEG-2 compression is applied end-to-end, encryption can be performed after compression without conflict. The payload type does not introduce non-uniform receiver-side computational complexity that would cause a denial-of-service threat. A security review found no additional considerations beyond those in the RTP specification.
sections.eli5: If you want privacy, encrypt the whole packet. The format itself does not create special security holes.

fields.name: Header Changed (N)
fields.desc: Set if sequence, GOP or picture headers differ from previous.

fields.name: Reserved (MBZ)
fields.desc: Must be zero. Reserved for future use.

fields.name: Audio Length
fields.desc: Bytes of audio data in this packet.

fields.name: Audio Offset
fields.desc: Offset in audio samples between audio frame start and RTP timestamp.
